tier_reason: The README Performance section has bar charts (docs/assets/bench_ondemand.png and bench_ondemand_find_tweet.png) comparing zimdjson with simdjson DOM/On-Demand and yyjson. The benchmark code is public (bench/<task>/*.zig and *.cpp, bench/runner.zig, build/bench.zig), but the CPU is given only as '3.30GHz Intel Skylake' with no model, and no Zig version or optimize mode is stated, so this is first-party partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: zimdjson (On-Demand) beats simdjson (On-Demand) on 3 of the 5 tasks in bench_ondemand.png: find-system ~1.74 vs ~1.17 GB/s (~1.5x), top-factions ~1.59 vs ~1.04 GB/s (~1.5x), coordinates ~1.63 vs ~1.06 GB/s (~1.5x). simdjson (On-Demand) is faster on top-tweet (~2.84 vs ~2.64 GB/s) and partial-tweets (~2.82 vs ~2.43 GB/s). Values are read off the bar chart, and the ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig build system (`zig build bench/...`) for all contenders. The simdjson and yyjson C++ benchmarks are compiled through Zig's addCSourceFile (Zig's bundled Clang) with the same standardOptimizeOption mode as the Zig code. The Zig version and optimize mode used for the published charts are not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own repo/author). Numbers are read off bar charts (images), not a table. The CPU is given only as '3.30GHz Intel Skylake' (no model). No Zig version or optimize mode is recorded with the results. The two charts disagree for the same tasks (for example, find-system zimdjson On-Demand is ~2.0 GB/s in bench_ondemand_find_tweet.png but ~1.74 GB/s in bench_ondemand.png), which suggests run-to-run variance. Results depend on the workload, not a uniform win: simdjson On-Demand wins both twitter.json tasks. The author's README note says 'do not trust any benchmark'. The last commit on the default branch is 2025-04-29, and the newest commit on any branch (0.15.x) is 2025-08-24.

tier_reason: bench/SIDE-BY-SIDE.md is a paired board: rxmlint against a pinned libxml2 v2.15.3 xmllint, with the harness public in bench/pinvs.ps1. No CPU model and no rustc version are stated, and the C side is a prebuilt oracle binary, so this is first-party partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: As shipped (rxmlint linked with rusty_alloc against xmllint on the system allocator), CLI parse-noout: 1.55x-2.31x faster (derived from page data). The us/C ratios are 0.447x on big-attr.xml (83.25 vs 37.18 MB/s), 0.644x on big-1m.xml (115.74 vs 74.56), 0.625x on big-300k.xml (125.56 vs 78.47) and 0.432x on slashdot.xml (118.05 vs 50.98). All four files show 20/20 paired wins at z=+4.47. The README headline is '1.6x to 2.2x faster'. With the same allocator on both sides (the parser alone, N=11), the page reports big-attr 0.80x (~1.25x faster, derived) and big-300k 1.07x (rusty_xml ~7% slower). The author states that roughly half the margin is the allocator.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rxmlint built with `cargo build -p rusty_xml-cli --release` (rustc version not stated) and linked with rusty_alloc. libxml2 is a pinned prebuilt v2.15.3 xmllint.exe on the system allocator. Parse options differ: C defaults to XML_PARSE_COMPACT | XML_PARSE_BIG_LINES, and rxmlint forces NONET | NO_XXE.
corrections.hardware: CPU model not stated. The harness is Windows PowerShell (xmllint.exe/rxmlint.exe), pinned to core 4 at High priority, and measures CPU time.
corrections.workload: CLI-vs-CLI parse without output (xmllint --noout against rxmlint --noout, --repeat inner loop) on big-attr.xml (627KB), big-1m.xml (1.27MB), big-300k.xml (309KB) and slashdot.xml (3.7KB x 10000). The run is single core, CPU-time metric, ABBA-interleaved, with N=20 pairs and a C-vs-C null arm per row.
corrections.caveats: The headline ratio is 'as shipped' and includes rusty_alloc (a pure-Rust mimalloc port) against libxml2 on the system allocator. With the same allocator, the author measures only 0.80x on big-attr and 1.07x on big-300k, where rusty_xml is slower, and says quoting the as-shipped ratio as a parser result would be wrong. The slashdot.xml row is flattered because xmllint re-opens and re-reads the file on every --repeat. This is CLI-vs-CLI with different parse flags, not a kernel A/B. The repo is very new (created 2026-08-27, 1 star). The CPU model, OS details and rustc version are not stated. The numbers are the author's own and are not independently reproduced.

notes: The numbers match SIDE-BY-SIDE.md and the README. The record left out the author's own same-allocator disclosure, which shows the parser alone is not uniformly faster (big-300k 1.07x, slower), so the claim was overstated. Tier C stays. License confirmed as MIT OR Apache-2.0 (LICENSE-MIT, LICENSE-APACHE and Cargo.toml; GitHub detects only Apache-2.0). Last commit 2026-09-20, not a fork.
